---
title: "Practical: write a physiological report"
---

## Purpose

A report should let a reader understand what was asked, how the observations
were obtained, what the results show and how far the physiological explanation
can go. Use one of the supplied analysis practicals or the instructor's actual
laboratory activity. This is a teaching template and feedback framework,
**not an approved grading scheme or official submission instruction**.
Write a first draft, then revise it after feedback.

No programming is required. A clear calculation table and labelled figure can
meet this activity's goals. If software is used, preserve source data and the
steps producing the result. The [worked-figure gallery](../figures.qmd) gives
examples for comparison after your own first attempt. Any formal assessment
follows the current course instructions.

## Report structure and prompts

### Title and question

Name the process, comparison and organism/system if known. “Lab report 2”
does not tell a reader what was investigated. End the introduction with one
answerable question and an explicit prediction justified by physiology.
Explain the essential mechanism in your own words before citing a reference.

For the simulated respirometry example, an appropriate question is whether
mass-specific oxygen consumption differs between the supplied temperature
groups. Calling the activity an experiment you personally carried out would
misrepresent its provenance.

### Methods and design

State whether observations are measured, supplied or simulated. Identify the
independent unit, allocation, conditions, measurement interval, controls,
variables and units. Define the calculation, including correction and
normalisation. Keep enough detail for the analysis to be reconstructed while
using the actual local protocol for live laboratory methods.

Write what happened, rather than a list of commands. Explain why the method
answers the question. If an assumption is stipulated in the exercise, identify
it as such; do not claim you verified calibration or randomisation in a dataset
you did not collect. Note missing observations and how they were handled.

### Results

Show individual observations where feasible, a relevant summary and one
worked calculation or sufficiently documented computational step. Every
figure needs axis labels, units and a caption identifying its units of
replication. Say whether uncertainty marks represent SD, SE or a confidence
interval. If there are no error bars, do not describe them.

State the direction and size of the comparison in words, using an explicit
subtraction order. “There was a difference” is incomplete; “the warm-group
mean was higher by 0.125 µmol O₂ min⁻¹ g⁻¹” specifies an interpretable
quantity in the respirometry example. Keep the simulated-data qualifier nearby.
No p-value is needed merely to make a report look scientific.

### Discussion

Answer the original question first. Connect the pattern to a plausible
mechanism, identifying which mechanistic variables were actually measured.
Discuss design limits, measurement limits and limits of generalisation.
Choose one concrete improvement linked to one limitation. “Use better
equipment” is less useful than specifying a calibration check or matched blank.

Separate absence of evidence from evidence of absence. A wide interval or
small sample may leave multiple effects compatible with observations.
Likewise, a large difference in a constructed example is not a biological
discovery. Do not translate respiration into growth, height into biomass,
or leaf gas exchange into field yield without evidence.

### References and provenance

Cite sources supporting mechanisms and definitions, using author/year or
another consistent style. Give direct source identifiers so a reader can
find them. Identify course-generated simulated data by file and dictionary.
Do not cite a paper as the origin of an invented dataset. Do not copy its
figure or legend unless reuse is permitted and attributed.

## Peer-review task

Exchange drafts. The reviewer should locate the independent unit, a unit-bearing
calculation, the main figure and the sentence answering the question. If any
cannot be found, ask for clarification rather than silently repairing it.
Write three short comments: one statement supported well, one ambiguity and
one specific revision that would improve physiological reasoning.

| Dimension | Evidence of a clear report | Revision needed if… |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Question and physiology | Question and prediction connect to a mechanism | A general topic replaces an answerable question |
| Design and measurement | Unit, conditions, controls and provenance are explicit | Repeated readings are counted as new organisms |
| Calculation and presentation | Units, correction, direction and individual values are clear | A result cannot be traced to observations |
| Interpretation | Size, mechanism and limitations are distinguished | A proxy or association is presented as proof of mechanism |
| Communication | Figures, captions, sources and writing support the argument | Formatting hides missing methods or unexplained claims |

These dimensions guide feedback; they assign neither marks nor grade boundaries.

## Final revision checklist

Can another person reconstruct one result from the source table? Can they tell
which organism or pot is independent? Does the figure support the reported
comparison? Do the question, calculation and conclusion use the same outcome?
Are simulated data identified? Is every cited source traceable? Does the
discussion name one uncertainty that matters to the conclusion?

Leave with a revised report, figure and original data, plus a note saying what
changed after feedback. If using R Markdown optionally, retain the `.Rmd` and
render after restarting R. Producing HTML is a reproducibility check, not
proof that the biological interpretation is correct.

Continue to [literature and presentation](literature-presentation.qmd) or the
[practical route](index.qmd).
